title: Where to Place a Demo Lead Form (Storylane Demo Suite)
summary: Where to place the lead-capture form in an interactive demo: a decision framework for mid vs end gating, with Storylane Demo Suite examples.
body_markdown:
Where to place the lead-capture form in an interactive demo is the wrong first question, and asking it first is exactly why so many teams end up with a demo that either leaks pipeline or scares visitors off. The right first question is what you actually want to learn from the demo, because that decides the placement, not the other way around. I am Madhav Bhandari, CMO at Storylane, and I have watched this call get made backwards more times than I can count.


The instinct is to gate everything up front so no lead escapes. The result is a bounce spike and a much shorter list of people who ever saw the product, which is the same dynamic behind[why contact forms suppress conversion](https://www.storylane.io/blog/why-contact-forms-suppress-conversion) . My position: for most demos the highest-converting default is a mid-demo cliff-hanger placed right after your aha moment, and a hard front gate should be the exception you can justify, not the reflex.


> **Definition:** Lead-capture form placement is the point in an interactive demo where you ask the visitor for contact details: before the demo (a pre-demo gate), partway through it (a mid-demo or cliff-hanger gate), or after it (an end gate or CTA).


## The three placement options, and why "where" is the wrong first question


Every on-topic guide names the same three positions.


A pre-demo gate asks for details before the visitor sees anything. A mid-demo gate interrupts at a chosen step, usually right before a high-value feature. An end gate waits until the tour is done and asks as part of the closing call to action.


That framing is necessary background, not the answer. Naming three doors tells you nothing about which one to open, and picking by gut feel is how teams either strangle their reach or flood the CRM with names that never convert. If you have not built the demo yet, start with[building your interactive demo](https://www.storylane.io/blog/how-to-create-an-interactive-product-demo) and treat placement as a later decision.


The deeper problem is that people reach for whatever lead tool is already nearby and assume it fits the demo journey. It rarely does. One buyer put it plainly:


> "I guess our website is in the process of being updated at the moment, but part of the journey, we use HubSpot and HubSpot's chatbot just isn't fit for purpose, never was." - \[Head of Sales, education technology\]


A tool built for website chat was never built to capture intent inside a guided product tour. That mismatch matters more now that 67% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free buying experience (Gartner, 2026). If they want to self-serve first, gating the front door defeats the point.


## What the data actually says about lead-capture form placement


The most-cited placement statistics on this topic come from demo vendors' own blogs, measured on their own customers with methodology you cannot inspect. I am not going to hand you a competitor's number and call it proof.


Treat every published placement stat, ours or anyone's, as directional until you have run it on your own demo.


What holds up is the mechanism, not the magic percentage. A mid-demo gate tends to beat a front gate because the visitor has already seen enough value to justify the ask, but has not yet disengaged.


> The moment to ask is when interest is highest and doubt is lowest. That is almost never step one, and it is often earlier than the final screen, where you have already lost the people who drifted off.


A front gate asks before you have earned it, so intent-poor visitors bounce and your finisher pool shrinks. An end gate asks after the peak, so you collect the diligent few and miss everyone who got their answer two steps early.


The cliff-hanger sits in the middle on purpose. The only way to know your exact peak is to look at where visitors drop off in your own analytics, which is the measurement work later in this piece.


## A decision framework for choosing your lead-capture form placement


This is the part no competitor page gives you: a way to match placement to the job the demo is doing. Placement is not a best practice you copy, it is a function of demo goal, funnel stage, and how identified the visitor already is. The higher the intent and the more you already know about the person, the more a gate costs you nothing.


Demo goal Where it lives Recommended placement Why


Top-of-funnel reach Embedded on a high-traffic blog post or landing page End gate or no gate Most visitors are anonymous and low-intent; optimize for how many see the product, capture at the end or identify silently


Mid-funnel qualification Self-serve trial alternative on the site Mid-demo cliff-hanger after the aha feature The visitor has seen real value but has not disengaged, so the ask converts and the lead is warm


Bottom-of-funnel sales enablement Follow-up demo sent to a named account Pre-demo gate, or no gate at all You already know who they are, so a gate costs almost nothing, and often you can skip it and track engagement against the known contact


The first row is where most reach demos live, and the pattern is covered in depth in[embedding a demo on your website to generate leads](https://www.storylane.io/blog/embed-a-product-demo-on-your-website-to-get-more-leads) . The third row is a common miss: teams re-gate a demo they emailed to a contact they already have, adding friction for zero information gain. If your goal is[turning demo requests into pipeline](https://www.storylane.io/blog/demo-requests) , the person is already identified, so spend your gate budget on routing speed, not on a redundant form.


## Placement by demo length and format


Length changes the math, because a gate needs runway in front of it. A micro-demo does not have room to build value before it interrupts, so a mid-flow gate there just annoys people. A long guided demo has plenty of runway, which is exactly where a cliff-hanger earns its keep.


Demo length Recommended placement Notes


Micro-demo (1 to 3 steps) End gate or no gate Too short to interrupt without breaking the experience; capture at the CTA or identify silently


Short demo (under 5 steps) End gate Not enough runway to build the value a mid-demo gate needs to feel earned


Long guided demo (5+ steps) Mid-demo cliff-hanger before advanced features Room to reach the aha moment first, then gate the payoff step


Format matters alongside length. A[guided demo format](https://www.storylane.io/blog/guided-demos-the-what-why-and-how) walks a viewer through a sequence, so it has a natural mid-point to gate, while a shorter[interactive product guide](https://www.storylane.io/blog/how-to-create-an-interactive-product-guide-for-your-saas-product) usually reads better with the ask at the end.


For anything genuinely short, treat[micro-demos](https://www.storylane.io/blog/micro-demos) as a no-gate surface whose job is reach. And a caveat worth repeating for anyone just starting: do not gate your very first demo at all. Learn where people drop off before you decide where to interrupt them.


## Alternative to gating: capturing leads without a form at all


Here is the option almost nobody mentions: you do not always need a form to capture a lead. A hard gate is one way to turn a visitor into a known contact, but it is the highest-friction way, and friction is why your finisher pool shrinks.


You can identify demand without asking a soul to type, and there are proven ways to[convert visitors without forms](https://www.storylane.io/blog/convert-visitors-without-forms) . The practical routes:


- Company-level identification by resolving the visitor's IP or domain, so you know which account is engaging even before anyone fills anything in.
- URL parameters and cookies passed from an email or ad, which tie the session to a known person automatically.
- Behavioral signal captured on the demo itself, so a sales team can prioritize the accounts spending real time in the product.


None of this replaces a form when you genuinely need a typed email and consent. It complements it.


The smart pattern is to identify silently on high-traffic, low-intent placements, and reserve the actual form for the moment intent peaks. That gives you coverage on the anonymous majority and a clean opt-in from the people worth a follow-up.


## Full disclosure: this is us


Full disclosure: this is us. Storylane Demo Suite is how we build the[interactive demos](https://www.storylane.io/interactive-demos) I have been describing, so I am not neutral. What I can tell you is the mechanism, not the pitch.


In Demo Suite you can drop a lead form at any step, gate a specific chapter, or run a demo fully ungated and still identify the visiting company by domain or IP. That is what makes the framework above executable rather than theoretical.


The part that actually changes the decision is step-level analytics. You can see where viewers drop off across Demo Hubs and Sandbox Demos, find where your real aha moment sits, and place the gate there instead of guessing. Keep any example data you show a prospect realistic and clearly labeled, because buyers notice immediately when demo analytics look invented.


Where it does not fit: if all you need is a booked-call form on a pricing page, a demo tool is overkill. And if your audience is non-technical and conservative, a heavy qualification-first gate can be too much, so favor a lighter-touch end gate or silent identification. Not every audience wants to be interrogated before they can look.


## How to measure whether your lead-capture form placement is working


Placement is not a one-time decision, it is a hypothesis you test. The only way to settle it for your demo is to run the options against each other and compare the outcomes that matter, not the ones that flatter you.


Here is a simple A/B test you can run on a single demo:


1. Duplicate the demo and change only the form position, nothing else.
2. Split traffic 50/50 on the same page and the same source, so intent is comparable.
3. Run until each variant has enough submissions to be meaningful, a few hundred sessions per arm as a rough floor.
4. Compare lead-to-opportunity rate, not raw submission count, because volume without quality is a trap, which is where[tying demo analytics to revenue attribution](https://www.storylane.io/blog/demo-analytics-revenue-attribution) earns its keep.
5. Keep the winner, then test the next variable rather than changing three things at once.


Watch these metrics per placement, and read them together:


Metric What it tells you


Completion rate Whether the gate is interrupting people before they finish


Lead-to-opportunity by placement Lead quality, not just how many forms got filled


Time-to-submission When intent actually peaks inside the demo


Form-view-to-submit rate How much friction the form itself is adding at that step


A worked example makes the trade-off concrete. Say an embedded demo gets 1,000 sessions a month.


With an end gate, 55% reach the end (550 finishers) and 8% of them submit, which is 44 leads. Move the ask to a cliff-hanger and 70% reach the gate step (700 viewers) with 9% submitting, which is 63 leads.


Same traffic, roughly 40% more leads, and because they raised their hand at a moment of interest, more are worth a call. Plug in your own rates before trusting anyone's headline number.


## Form design basics that apply regardless of placement


Wherever the form sits, keep it small. For most demos, a name and a work email is enough to route and follow up, and every field you add past that lowers completion. Add a field only when the routing genuinely needs it, not because a spreadsheet somewhere has a column for it.


A few rules that hold across every placement:


- Ask for name and work email by default, and justify any field beyond those two.
- Include an explicit opt-in for consent wherever your market requires it.
- Pre-fill known fields when the visitor is already identified, so you never make a known contact retype what you already have.
- Match the copy to the moment, so a mid-demo ask references the feature they are about to unlock rather than a generic "get in touch."


This is table stakes, and it is well covered everywhere, so I will not pad it. The point is simply that good form hygiene will not rescue a bad placement, and a great placement will still underperform behind a bloated seven-field form. Get the position right first, then keep the form as light as the situation allows.


## Conclusion


Where to place the lead-capture form in an interactive demo comes down to one honest answer: it depends on what the demo is for. Match placement to demo goal, funnel stage, and length, default to a mid-demo cliff-hanger when you have the runway, and reserve the front gate for visitors you already know. On high-traffic, low-intent surfaces, lean toward an end gate or silent identification, and let the anonymous majority see the product before you ask them for anything.


The teams that win this are not the ones with the cleverest single placement. They are the ones who treat placement as a testable hypothesis, watch lead quality rather than raw form fills, and let their own drop-off data decide.


Run the test, keep the winner, and move on to the next variable. That discipline, more than any position on the screen, is what turns a demo into pipeline.


## FAQ


**Should I gate my demo at all?**


Not always. If the demo's job is reach, an ungated demo with silent company identification usually generates more pipeline than a hard gate. For the full case on[whether you should gate your interactive demos](https://www.storylane.io/blog/should-you-gate-your-interactive-demos) at all, weigh reach against capture first. Gate when you need a typed email and consent, and place that gate where intent peaks rather than at the front door.


**What is a cliff-hanger placement?**


A cliff-hanger gate interrupts the demo partway through, right before a high-value feature, and asks for details to continue. It works because the visitor has seen enough to want more but has not disengaged, so the ask feels earned.


**How many form fields should an interactive demo ask for?**


For most demos, name and work email is enough to route and follow up. Every extra field lowers completion, so add one only when your routing genuinely depends on it.


**Can I combine multiple form placements in one demo?**


Yes, and it often works well. A common pattern is silent company identification throughout plus a single typed form at the peak-intent step. Avoid stacking multiple hard gates, since each one sheds viewers.


**Does gating hurt SEO or shareability of an embedded demo?**


A hard front gate reduces how many people engage with an embedded demo, which weakens the on-page signals search engines reward and makes it less shareable. An end gate or no gate keeps the experience open, so favor lighter placement on public, discovery-focused pages.
